Florence, February. Karl has to write his first formal email to a parish priest from a church near Siena, to send him the results of the analyses. Chiara reads over his shoulder.
I wrote: "Hi don Paolo, here are the results. Bye, Karl." Is that OK?
Karl! He's a parish priest, not a university friend. You start with "Dear don Paolo" or "Reverend".
Then you explain why you're writing. "I hereby send you the results of the analyses of the Madonna in your church."
Yes, in formal letters it's often written like that. It's a form of respect. Then: "Please find attached the full report."
And if I want to ask him to come and see the painting?
You use the conditional: "Would it be possible to meet next week?" Never "Come here".
And how do I close? "Bye" isn't right, I imagine.
"I remain available for any clarification. Kind regards." And then the signature, with the name of the cooperative.
In Maltese three lines were enough. In Italian you need a treatise.
Welcome to Italy, Karl. Here even a letter is a work of art. Or at least, a restoration.
Gentile signora Rossi, / Gentile dottor Gori,
Reverendo don Paolo, / Gentile don Paolo,
"Gentile" is the safest formula, for men and women. "Egregio" is more solemn and only for men. "Spettabile" (Spett.le) is used for companies.
Con la presente Le comunico che…
in riferimento a / a seguito di
In riferimento alla Sua email del 3 marzo…
Mi permetto di sollecitare una risposta.
"Mi permetto di sollecitare" = may I remind you. It's the polite way of saying "you still haven't replied".
Le sarei grato se potesse rispondermi entro venerdì.
The conditional softens the request. "Le sarei grato / grata se" + congiuntivo imperfetto is the most elegant formula.
Resto in attesa di un Suo cortese riscontro.
Rimango a disposizione per qualsiasi chiarimento.
I remain available for any clarification.

Thanking you for your attention, I send my regards.
Never "Ciao" or "Baci" in a formal email. And don't forget the subject (l'oggetto): "Oggetto: Risultati analisi — Madonna della pieve di San Leonardo".
5. The present participle in bureaucratic language
The present participle (-ante, -ente) often appears as a noun or adjective in documents:
Il richiedente deve firmare il modulo.
La parte interessata riceverà una copia.
Many present participles have become ordinary nouns: il cantante, il presidente, lo studente, l'insegnante. You already know them!

In February the Ernesto cooperative discovered a kind of work that none of the partners had foreseen: letters. Ever since Mancini had written the article about the Madonna from Siena, dozens of emails arrived every morning. Priests asking for quotes, museums wanting information, dioceses sending forms to fill in, students asking to do an internship, journalists wanting an interview. And every email wanted a reply. A formal reply, in correct Italian, with the right formulas. Matei, who wrote very well in Romanian, wrote in Italian the way he spoke. Giulia wrote well, but slowly. Chiara was good, but had no time. And Karl, the new intern, wrote in "chat" Italian.

The first disaster came on 12 February. Karl had to send the results of the analyses to don Paolo, the priest of the country church of San Leonardo, near Siena, the one where he had discovered the fourteenth-century pigment under the eighteenth-century Madonna. It was the most important news of his life, and he wrote it in three lines: "Hi don Paolo! Here are the results, the Madonna is older than we thought. Cool, right? Bye, Karl." Chiara read it over his shoulder just in time, a second before he pressed "send". She sat down beside him, took a deep breath and said: "Karl. We need to talk."

Karl tried to defend himself. He said that in Malta, at university, he wrote like that even to his professors, and nobody had ever been offended. He said that email English was fast and practical, and that long formulas seemed a waste of time to him. Chiara listened to the end, then opened her computer and looked for an old email, from seven years before. It was the first one she had written to the director of the Opificio, when she was twenty-two and asking for an internship. It began with "Hi prof" and ended with "Thanks a lot, see you soon!!!", with three exclamation marks. "He never replied," said Chiara. "Two months later I rewrote everything with 'Dear Director' and 'yours faithfully'. He called me the next day." Karl looked at the screen for a long time. Then he asked, in a whisper, whether he could copy the second version.

That evening, at the trattoria, there took place what Pietro later called "the first lesson of the via Maggio school of letters". Chiara explained the rules to Karl. The greeting: "Dear", never "Hi". The capital of courtesy: "Le scrivo", "la Sua email". The opening formulas: "hereby", "with reference to". The conditional for requests: "would it be possible", "I would be grateful if". And the closing: "I look forward to hearing from you", "kind regards". Karl took notes with the face of someone learning a new language. "In Maltese," he said at one point, "a letter like this would be an insult. It would look as if you were making fun of the recipient."

Graziella, who was listening from the kitchen, intervened with her usual wisdom. "In Italy," she said, "formal letters serve one purpose only: to make the other person understand that you respect them, even if you don't know them. My dad, when he wrote to the council for the trattoria licence, took a week. He began with 'Most illustrious Mr Mayor' and ended with 'with respect'. And the licence always arrived. The neighbour, who wrote 'Dear Mayor, I need the licence, thanks', waited two years." Karl laughed. Then he wrote in his notebook, under the list of formulas: "Con osservanza (with respect) = old. Don't use. But it works."

At that point Matei too confessed his sins. He told them that, in his first year in Florence, he had written to the bank about a current account starting with "Egregio signora", because he didn't know that "egregio" isn't used for women. The branch manager had replied with a very kind email, which began with "Dear Mr Popa" and ended with a sentence he hadn't understood: "Thank you for your originality". Giulia, who didn't know the story, laughed until she cried. Then she confessed too: in Naples, as a student, she had signed a request to the university with "Hugs, Giulia". Graziella shook her head, amused. "You see?" she said. "Nobody is born knowing how to write a letter. You learn by making mistakes. The important thing is to make mistakes with the right people, before you make them with the bishop."

The letter to don Paolo, rewritten that evening, filled a whole page. "Dear don Paolo, I hereby send you the results of the analyses carried out on the Madonna in your church. Please find attached the full report. As you will read, the analyses have revealed, under the eighteenth-century painting, the presence of a fourteenth-century pigment, which suggests a work much older than was believed. Would it be possible to meet next week, so that I can present the results to you in person? I remain available for any clarification. Kind regards, Karl Borg, Ernesto Restoration Cooperative."

Don Paolo replied the next morning, at half past seven. His reply was twice as long, written in an even more formal Italian, with sentences that began with "Thanking you most sincerely" and ended with "looking forward to meeting you, I send you my most cordial greetings in the Lord". In the middle, however, there was a sentence that made the whole workshop shout for joy: "The diocese is willing to fund the complete restoration of the work, should your cooperative wish to submit a quote." Karl read the reply three times. Then he looked at Chiara. "You were right," he said. "With 'Hi' he would never have replied like that."

From that day on, Karl became the most fanatical writer of formal letters in the cooperative. He wrote to everyone with the same care: to priests, to museums, to paint suppliers, even to the plumber who had to fix the workshop sink, who received an email beginning "Dear Sirs, with reference to the fault reported today". The plumber phoned Chiara to ask whether the workshop had been bought by a multinational. Chiara explained that no, it was just a Maltese intern who had discovered Italian bureaucracy and fallen in love with it.

So as not to forget anything, Karl also prepared a "handbook": a laminated sheet, pinned with four drawing pins next to the workshop computer. It was divided into four columns, with titles written in red: "How to begin", "How to ask", "How to attach", "How to close". Under each title were the formulas, from the simplest to the most solemn, and next to each one a small symbol: a sun for emails to colleagues, a tie for clients, a bishop's mitre for the diocese. At the bottom of the sheet, in small letters, Karl had added a fifth column, entitled "Never": "Ciao", "Baci", "Figo", three exclamation marks. Within a week, everyone in the workshop was using it. Even Chiara, who would never have admitted it, glanced at it before writing to the Soprintendenza.

Pietro too, that winter, wrote his first formal letter. It was to Professor Ruggeri, in Rome, and Bellini had suggested it. In the spring, in fact, Ruggeri and Giulia were going to Malta for the analysis of the T, and Pietro wanted to ask permission to attend. It took him three evenings to write it. He rewrote it six times. He had it read by Bellini, Chiara, Karl, his grandmother, even Davide, who said it was "too long but very beautiful". In the end the letter said: "Dear Professor Ruggeri, I take the liberty of writing to ask whether it would be possible to attend the analysis of the T, as an observer. I undertake not to touch anything and not to ask questions, unless strictly necessary."

Ruggeri's reply arrived two days later, and it was the shortest Pietro had ever received from an adult. "Dear Pietro, I have received your letter, which is better written than many degree theses I read every year. The answer is yes. But on one condition: you must ask the questions. Especially those that are not strictly necessary. Those are the ones that lead to discoveries. Kind regards, Ruggeri." Pietro printed it and stuck it in the black notebook, next to the dedication in Bellini's book. Then he noticed something, and showed it to Bellini: Ruggeri had addressed him with "Lei", with a capital letter. A fourteen-year-old boy. Bellini smiled. "It's the greatest compliment a university professor can pay," he said.

Not all letters, however, ended well. At the end of February an email arrived from a large company in Milan, which handled restorations on behalf of banks and insurers. It was signed by a certain Dr Ferraris, sales director, and was written in impeccable Italian, as cold as marble. "We hereby inform you of our interest in acquiring your cooperative, on terms we consider advantageous. Please find attached a preliminary proposal. We look forward to your reply by 15 March." The attachment contained a figure with so many zeros that Chiara had to count them twice.

That evening, at the trattoria, there was a heavy silence. Nobody had expected it. A company from Milan, once again, wanting to buy something in via Maggio. Graziella put down the ladle and said only: "Again?" Matei read the proposal aloud. It was generous, honestly. Enough to pay off the bank loan in a day, and to let all three partners live comfortably for years. In return, the cooperative would change its name, become "a Tuscan branch of the group", and work mainly for banks and private collections. "No more country churches," said Giulia quietly. "No more don Paolo."

They discussed it for three days. Matei was tempted: he thought of Viola, of school, of the future. Chiara was against it: she said she had worked all her life so as not to depend on anyone. Giulia didn't know. Bellini, when they asked him, answered only that the workshop was no longer his, and that they had to decide. But on the evening of the third day he left a sealed envelope on the workshop table, addressed "To the Ernesto cooperative". Inside was a photocopy of the first page of Ernesto's diary, the one from 1946, when he had reopened the workshop after the war. At the top, written in pencil, there was a single sentence: "We work for those who need it, not for those who can pay the most."

The next day, Karl wrote the reply. The partners had asked him to, because by now he was the best letter writer in the workshop. It took him all morning, and he had everyone read it before sending it. "Dear Sirs, with reference to your kind proposal of 26 February, we thank you most sincerely for the interest shown in our cooperative. After careful consideration, we must nevertheless decline the offer. Our cooperative bears the name of a restorer who worked for those who needed it, and we wish to continue to do so. We remain available for any future collaboration. Yours faithfully, Ernesto Restoration Cooperative."

Dr Ferraris's reply came an hour later, and it surprised everyone. It was only two lines long, and for the first time it contained not a single bureaucratic formula. "I read your letter three times. My grandfather was a restorer in Bergamo, and he used to say the same thing. If one day you need anything, call me. Ferraris." Karl read it aloud, and in the workshop nobody said anything for a long moment. Then Chiara burst out laughing. "You see, Karl?" she said. "Formal letters serve to make the other person understand that you respect them. But every now and then, if you write them well, they also make them remember who their grandfather was."

This time it was Matei who wrote the reply, and he decided not to use the handbook. He wrote just four lines, without "Dear Sirs" and without "yours faithfully", the way you write to a person and not to a group. "Dear Dr Ferraris, your email moved us more than your proposal. If one day you're passing through Florence, come and visit us in via Maggio. We'll show you Ernesto's diary, and Signora Graziella will offer you a ribollita. It's not a quote: it's an invitation. Matei Popa." Karl, who was reading over his shoulder, protested that at least three compulsory formulas were missing. Matei smiled and pressed "send". "The handbook is for people you don't know," he told him. "When someone tells you about their grandfather, you already know them."

The following week, Karl went with Chiara to the country church of San Leonardo, near Siena, to meet don Paolo. He was an eighty-year-old priest, small and very thin, with a worn cassock and very lively eyes, who was waiting for them at the church door with a tray of cantucci. "Ah, you're the young man of the letters," he said to Karl, shaking his hand. "I took the liberty of reading your first email to the bishop. He told me he hadn't received such a well-written letter since 1985." Karl blushed. Chiara nudged him, smiling. Then they went into the church, and don Paolo led them to the Madonna, who had been waiting for them in the half-light for seven hundred years.

That evening, back in Florence, Karl wrote one last letter. It wasn't formal. It was to his mother, in Malta, and he wrote it by hand, in Maltese, on a sheet of paper he had bought specially from a stationer's in via Maggio. He told her about the letters, about don Paolo, about Dr Ferraris, about Ernesto's sentence. At the end, after his signature, he added a line in Italian, because it wouldn't come to him in Maltese: "I look forward to hearing from you." He knew his mother wouldn't understand. But he also knew she would ask someone to translate it for her, and that she would laugh. And he was right: his mother's reply, two weeks later, began with "Dear son" — in the most formal Italian.

In March, on the workshop wall, next to Davide's drawing and the photo of the banner, a new frame appeared. Inside were three letters, side by side. The first was Karl's wrong one to don Paolo, printed before Chiara stopped him: "Hi don Paolo! Cool, right?". The second was the corrected one, a whole page long. The third was Dr Ferraris's reply, two lines long. Under the frame, Pietro had written a title in his neatest handwriting: "Three ways of writing a letter. The first is wrong. The second is correct. The third is true."

When Bellini saw it, on Saturday morning, he stood in front of the frame for a long time, with his hands behind his back. Then he called Pietro. "The fourth way is missing," he said. Pietro looked at him without understanding. Bellini took out of his pocket the envelope he had left on the table a week earlier, the one with the photocopy of Ernesto's diary, and pinned it with a drawing pin next to the other three. Below, he wrote in pencil, in small letters: "The fourth way: a single sentence, written for those who will come after." Pietro read Ernesto's sentence for the umpteenth time. "We work for those who need it, not for those who can pay the most." Then he copied it into his diary, word for word, as he did with Grandpa Aldo's sentences.
